sentences.text: 1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.
The accused no. 1 is stated to be the vendor of accused no. 3 business concern of which accused no. 2 is stated to be the proprietor.

The food article lifted for sampling is 'Rasgulla'.

sentences.text: As per the complaint, on 05.12.2007, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Shyam Lal and Field Assistant (FA) Siya Ram under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. N. K. Sharma reached along with their staff at the premises of accused no. 3 M/s.
Durga Sweets
Corner at 2411, Kamra Bangash, Daryaganj, Delhi, where the accused no. 1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption
. The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Rasgulla from the vendor, to which he had agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the notice as per Form-VI,
panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 27.12.2007, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it contained added starch which was not declared as an ingredient.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
It was found that the accused no. 2 was the proprietor of accused no. 3 business concern.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 18.07.2009 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 18.07.2009.

4. In the meanwhile, the accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to the CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 05.09.2009, opining the sample to be not conforming to the PFA Rules due to presence of 123.91 ppm of Sulphur dioxide being more than the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm.

5. Based on the report of the CFL, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against all the accused persons on 02.01.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
6. At the trial, prosecution examined three witnesses in support of its case.
PW-1 was the FI, PW-2 was the FA and PW-3 was the SDM/LHA who were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 05.12.2007 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Rasgulla, dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles, adding formalin (40 drops each) as preservative, fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.
They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, notice Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex. PW- 1/C, PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/E and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/F.

2 to STO during investigation to ascertain constitution of vendor business concern.
Accused no. 2 also gave his reply Ex. PW-1/I.
Sanction
Ex . PW-1/J was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/H (sic) was then filed in the court.
Intimation letter Ex. PW-1/K was then sent to the accused persons with copy of PA report vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/M.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the spoon / bottles used in the proceedings were not clean and dry.
The witnesses however, accepted that accused no. 2 was not present at the spot.
7. Statements of the accused persons under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 14.10.2013 wherein they denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Though they admitted the proceedings dated 05.12.2007, yet he denied the presence of SDM/LHA.
They claimed that no efforts were made to join public witnesses and that the price of sample was not paid.
They took stand that the reports of chemical experts are wrong, on the ground that representative samples were not taken by the food officials.
They chose not to lead evidence in defence.

8. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused have not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 05.09.2009 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

9. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses.

Ld. Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore,
conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report.
He has relied upon the various judgements in his support.
It is further contended that there is no standard prescribed for Rasgulla as a food article and in the absence of prescribed standard, it cannot be said that any Rule has been violated.
10. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
11. It is to be understood that the notice framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of the PFA Act.
This is important to note because the ingredients of these offences are different and distinct.

12. Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature,
substance or quality which it purported or represented to be. Section 2(ia)
(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Jeet Saini on 25 April, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172322847/
3 variability.
13.

sentences.text: In the case at hand, it is an admitted position, as is clear from both the reports of PA and CFL that the food article did not fall under any item of Appendix-B of the PFA Rules.
No standard has been prescribed under the Rules with respect to 'Rasgulla' as a food article as such.
It was thus analysed as a proprietary food.
Proprietary Food, as per Rule 37-A of PFA Rules means a food which has not been standardised under the said Rules.
Under Rule 37-A(e), proprietary food product shall not contain food additives except as provided under the rules for that food or category of food.
14. As per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.
As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and conclusive evidence for the facts stated therein.
Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.

15. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.
16.

entities.text: Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents.

entities.text: Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Director is a greater expert and therefore the statute says that his certificate shall be accepted by the court as conclusive evidence.
For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director....
Superseded is a strong word.
It means obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal.
The Director's cetificate supersedes the report given by the public analyst.
Once superseded it does not survive for any purpose.

It will be anamolous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded."
17.
In the case at hand, the PA report nowhere shows any analysis for presence of sulphur dioxide.
Thus, it cannot be said that sulphur dioxide was absent in that sample or any test gave negative result for the same.
Rather no test at all appears to have been performed by the PA to determine presence of sulphur dioxide.
Similar is the position with CFL report, where there is no report about any positive or negative result for starch.
It cannot be said if starch was present or not in that sample, as no test appears to have been performed to determine its presence.

18. Whatever might be the position, since the report of CFL is final and conclusive and the same supersedes the report of PA, only this report has to be considered and the report of PA has to be ignored.
As there is no report of presence of starch in CFL report, the matter has to be determined only on the basis of presence of sulphur dioxide.

sentences.text: It is not the case of the prosecution that sulphur dioxide is a prohibited substance or that its use in preparation of Rasgullas is not permitted.
The basis on which the Director CFL gave his report, is that the content of sulphur dioxide was found to be 123.91 ppm which is more than the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm.
20. Well, the prosecution has failed to show how this maximum limit of 100 ppm has been ascertained.
No specific Rule has been shown to exist that shows that this is the maximum permitted value in case of Rasgulla as a food article.
As already mentioned, Rasgulla is a proprietary food which is not a standardized food article.
Then it is not explained on what basis the maximum limit of 100 ppm is claimed to exist in this case.
21. Rules show that sulphur dioxide is a Class-II Preservative permitted for use in food articles, as per prescribed standards.
Its use is permitted in Sugar as an additive within prescribed limits.
But there is nothing to show that any such limit has been prescribed in case of Rasgullas lying open.
Rule 55 of PFA Rules mentions the group of foods for which limits are prescribed for use of preservatives.
It is in this Rule that Item 11-A deals with 'Canned Rasagolla' and Item 31 deals with 'Dry mixes of Rasagollas' in which case, 100 ppm of sulphur dioxide is permitted.
22. But it is nowhere the case of the complainant / prosecution that the Rasgullas in this case fell in any of these categories.
There is nothing to show that the Rasgullas lifted in this case were dry mixes or sugar syrup dipped.
The lifted Rasgullas were certainly not canned Rasgullas.

Thus, there is no standard fixed in case of open rasgullas so as to bring the matter within purview of section 2(ia) (m)
of PFA Act.
23.

The fact now to be determined is if the case falls in section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.
24.
As already noted, the prosecution has failed to show that use of sulphur dioxide in Rasgullas in question is limited upto 100 ppm.

And if there is no such maximum limit prescribed anywhere for use in this food article, and this substance is not a prohibited substance for use in Rasgullas or in sugar syrup ordinary used in Rasgullas, it cannot be said that presence of 123.91 ppm of sulphur dioxide can be said to be not of the nature, substance or quality demanded by the purchaser to his prejudice or is not of nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be, so as to bring it within the purview of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.

25. Therefore, when the prosecution has failed to explain as to how the limit of 100 ppm, as shown in CFL report, has been determined to exist in the case of Ragullas, it cannot be said that there is violation of any Rule or prescribed limits.

The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the sample in question was 'adulterated' within the meaning of section 2(ia) of PFA Act and thus, no case would be made out against the accused for commission of offences punishable under section 7/16 of the PFA Act.
26.
Having said so, the accused persons are entitled to be given the benefit of doubt.
They are therefore acquitted of the charges.
However, their bail bonds shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A. CrPC.
